extracted.intended_audience: aspiring joke-makers, humorists, writers and performers of comedy, and readers interested in humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical guidance for composing, diagnosing, and distinguishing good and bad jokes; outlines laws governing when jokes will produce laughter and what makes them fail. Emphasizes poetic vs. practical humor, audience interest, spontaneity, and the relation of disappointment to satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real engagement of the audience's interest (Law Number One)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a real engagement of the interest of the person who is expected to laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is a feeling and a play instinct, not merely an intellectual product. Jokes fail if the audience is not emotionally or volitionally alert; perfunctory kidding, conversational clowning, or relying solely on the form of comicality will not produce genuine laughter. Practically: ensure the company is disposed toward you and interested in the matter; use attribution tricks (crediting a famous humorist or claiming personal origin) to warm the audience—but be prepared to stand by the story if someone calls it. The chapter calls this principle 'humor must be alive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'rich' joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A rich joke is a poetic-practical joke in which both the interest balked (negative current) and the interest satisfied (positive current) are strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich jokes require at least two strong, opposing currents of feeling in the hearer (e.g., ambivalence about marriage, mixed feelings about doctors). Examples: jokes about matrimony (many people are both for and against) or the reinforced-point joke (man with appendix removed twice—the repeated detail intensifies the satisfaction). Avoid topics where interest flows only one way (e.g., many mothers-in-law jokes are not 'rich').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive emotional intensity (Law Number Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: The feelings aroused in the person who is expected to laugh must not be too strong and deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is play; subjects that touch deep passion or solemn satisfaction are unplayful and can make jokes seem inept or malapropos. Joking at moments of true grief or about profoundly charged matters can turn jokes into tragedies. Common failures under this law include hostile jokes carried too far and obscene/sexual jokes that revert to infantile contempt. Language choices matter: words indicate attitudes and can make sexual material feel blasphemous or crude rather than poetic. Only those who can command the audience's feelings should risk joking in deeply emotional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural induction of negative and positive currents (Law Number Three)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the negative (interest thwarted) and the positive (interest satisfied) currents of feeling must be simply and naturally induced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There should be no appearance of effort in building up the expectation or contriving the satisfaction. A joke must not seem manufactured, far-fetched, or labored; humor dies if the audience detects the maker 'working' at it. Avoid contrivance and overt construction—spontaneity of feeling is essential. Example anti-pattern: Mark Twain's famously labored speech that produced chilling silence; labored comic attempts feel like work rather than play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate and perfect identity of the positive with the negative (Law Number Four)
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction must be, or be of, or be in, the disappointment: the positive current must be immediate and identical with the negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke with a point must deliver its satisfaction instantly within the disappointed expectation—there must be no mediation, bridging, or need for explanation. Brevity and instant flash are essential. Do not explain or 'nurse' a lame joke; explanations make it lamer. Forced jokes that require an act of inference to join the two currents are imperfect. Examples of failures: explained/translated jokes that lose force; Shakespearean lines where wordplay is forced ('too' vs. 'to a'); headline jokes that depend on cultural knowledge may not flash for all audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic humor: perspective-shifting and enduring, point-less laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic jokes often provoke laughter without an explicit point by perceiving the world from an unexpected or shifted viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic humor arises from the imaginative sympathy that lets one see ordinary things in many different ways; such perception can produce enduring laughter even absent a pointed punchline. Examples: seeing Turner's painting as either 'The Slave-Ship' or 'a tortoiseshell cat having a fit in a platter of tomatoes'; a childlike romantic view upset by a realist's aside (elephant whose pants are falling down). Poetic humorists can fall back on the flow of materials and 'horse-play' when sharper incongruities fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the poetic humorist (persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic 'humorist' persona: a droll, uncouth magnetism that makes everything seem funny by being inappropriately natural rather than performing clownish tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humorist is distinct from satirists, clowns, or comedians; he makes topics funny because of his own inappropriate presence and a kind of lovable, provincial honesty. This persona does not rely on cracking jokes about subjects; instead, the humor springs from the speaker's character. Historical exemplars: Artemus Ward, Mark Twain—whose innocence and provincialism attack cultural elegance. For writers/performers: cultivating a believable, unstudied persona can render material inherently comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of humor distinctions (useful axes for classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several important distinctions for understanding and classifying humorous material: simple humor vs. jokes with a point; positive vs. negative currents; poetic vs. practical; quantitative vs. qualitative; dry vs. wet; salt wit vs. sweet; comic action vs. verbally conveyed humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axes provide foundations for systematic analysis of jokes and humor styles and explain why different audiences respond differently. The text warns that excessive scholastic classification can become absurd (laughing at anything when one is frivolized), but that the distinctions legitimately ground many permutations and combinations of comic forms. Use them to diagnose kinds of jokes and their likely effects.
